```{r packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
```

## Overview

An independent mini-project that combines the three core skills of the module on
a small environmental-health scenario: **fine particulate matter (PM2.5)
monitoring** at five urban sites.

PM2.5 (particles smaller than 2.5 µm) penetrates deep into the lungs and the
bloodstream, and it is one of the most studied components of the human
*exposome*. Monitoring networks compare daily readings against a reference
value; here we use the WHO 24-hour guideline of **15 µg/m³**. A reading
**exceeds** the guideline when it is *strictly greater* than 15 µg/m³.

| Part | Topic | Main tools |
|:----:|:------|:-----------|
| 1 | Data audit, control flow | `for`, `while`, `if`/`else` |
| 2 | A validated summary function | functions, input checks, Roxygen2 |
| 3 | SQL queries on the readings | `DBI`, `RSQLite`, `JOIN`, `HAVING` |
| 4 | Probability and simulation | binomial, Poisson, normal, hypergeometric |

> **Data note.** The dataset is **synthetic** and generated reproducibly below
> (`set.seed`). It mimics real monitoring problems (missing values, sensor
> errors, borderline readings) but contains no real measurements.

## Data generation

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)

sites <- c("Harbour", "Old Town", "Industrial Park", "Hillside", "Riverside")
median_pm25 <- c(14, 12, 19, 8, 11)          # typical level of each site (ug/m3)
n_per_site <- 24

readings <- data.frame(
  reading_id = sprintf("PM%03d", 1:(length(sites) * n_per_site)),
  site       = rep(sites, each = n_per_site),
  pm25       = round(rlnorm(length(sites) * n_per_site,
                            meanlog = log(rep(median_pm25, each = n_per_site)),
                            sdlog   = 0.45), 1)
)

# Inject typical data-quality problems
readings$pm25[c(5, 31, 58, 90)] <- NA        # missing values (sensor offline)
readings$pm25[c(14, 77)]        <- c(-1.0, -3.2)  # physically impossible (sensor error)
readings$pm25[40]               <- 15        # borderline reading, exactly at the limit
readings$pm25[1:3]              <- c(11.2, 8.6, 13.9)  # first days below the limit

sites_info <- data.frame(
  site      = sites,
  zone_type = c("Port", "Residential", "Industrial", "Residential", "Residential"),
  residents = c(12, 35, 4, 9, 21)            # thousands of residents
)
```

---

# Part 1. Programming fundamentals

## 1.1 Data audit

> Show the structure of `readings`. Count the missing values and the negative
> values, and explain why `na.rm = TRUE` is needed for the second count.

```{r audit}
str(readings)

n_missing  <- sum(is.na(readings$pm25))
n_negative <- sum(readings$pm25 < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

c(missing = n_missing, negative = n_negative)
```

A comparison such as `pm25 < 0` returns `NA` for a missing reading, and `sum()`
of a vector that contains `NA` is `NA`. With `na.rm = TRUE` the missing values
are skipped, so only real negative readings are counted. The data contain
`r n_missing` missing and `r n_negative` negative readings out of
`r nrow(readings)`.

## 1.2 Classification with a `for` loop

> Build a vector `status` with one label per reading: `"missing"` if the value
> is `NA`, `"sensor_error"` if it is negative, `"exceedance"` if it is strictly
> above 15 and `"compliant"` otherwise. Count how many readings fall in each
> category **inside the same loop**, using a named vector as counter.

```{r for-loop}
limit <- 15
status <- character(nrow(readings))
counts <- c(missing = 0, sensor_error = 0, exceedance = 0, compliant = 0)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(readings))) {
  if (is.na(readings$pm25[i])) {
    status[i] <- "missing"
  } else if (readings$pm25[i] < 0) {
    status[i] <- "sensor_error"
  } else if (readings$pm25[i] > limit) {
    status[i] <- "exceedance"
  } else {
    status[i] <- "compliant"
  }
  counts[status[i]] <- counts[status[i]] + 1
}

counts
sum(counts) == nrow(readings)   # every reading belongs to exactly one category
```

The `is.na()` check must come **first**: any comparison with `NA` returns `NA`,
and `if (NA)` stops with an error. The borderline reading of exactly 15 µg/m³
is classified as `compliant`, because the exceedance rule is strictly `> 15`.

## 1.3 First exceedance with a `while` loop

> Use a `while` loop to find the position of the first exceedance and report how
> many readings were processed before it.

```{r while-loop}
i <- 1
while (i <= nrow(readings) && status[i] != "exceedance") {
  i <- i + 1
}

if (i <= nrow(readings)) {
  cat("First exceedance:", readings$reading_id[i],
      "at", readings$site[i], "with", readings$pm25[i], "ug/m3\n")
  cat("Readings processed before it:", i - 1, "\n")
} else {
  cat("No exceedance found\n")
}
```

The condition `i <= nrow(readings)` is written **first** so that, when no
exceedance exists, the loop stops at the end of the data instead of indexing
beyond the last row. Unlike a `for` loop, a `while` loop needs the counter to be
initialised and updated by hand; forgetting `i <- i + 1` would loop forever.

# Part 2. A validated summary function

## 2.1 Definition

> Write `exposure_summary(x, limit = 15)`. It receives a vector of PM2.5
> readings and returns a list with the number of readings, the mean, the median,
> the 95th percentile and the percentage of readings strictly above `limit`.
> It must return an informative text message if `x` is not a non-empty numeric
> vector without missing or negative values, or if `limit` is not a single
> positive number.

```{r function}
#' Summarise PM2.5 exposure readings
#'
#' @param x Numeric vector of PM2.5 readings (ug/m3). It must be non-empty and
#'   contain no missing or negative values.
#' @param limit Single positive number used as the exceedance threshold.
#'   Defaults to the WHO 24-hour guideline (15 ug/m3).
#'
#' @return A list with `n_readings`, `mean`, `median`, `p95` and
#'   `percent_above` (percentage of readings strictly above `limit`).
#'   If an input check fails, a character message is returned instead.
exposure_summary <- function(x, limit = 15) {
  # Check the readings
  if (!is.numeric(x) || length(x) == 0) {
    return("Invalid input: x must be a non-empty numeric vector")
  }
  if (anyNA(x) || any(x < 0)) {
    return("Invalid input: x cannot contain missing or negative values")
  }

  # Check the limit (type and length first, sign last)
  if (!is.numeric(limit) || length(limit) != 1 || is.na(limit) || limit <= 0) {
    return("Invalid input: limit must be a single positive number")
  }

  list(
    n_readings    = length(x),
    mean          = mean(x),
    median        = median(x),
    p95           = unname(quantile(x, probs = 0.95)),
    percent_above = sum(x > limit) * 100 / length(x)
  )
}
```

## 2.2 Applying and testing it

> Apply the function to the valid readings of each site and test the edge cases.

```{r function-use}
valid_readings <- readings %>%
  filter(!is.na(pm25), pm25 >= 0)

# One summary per site
by_site <- t(sapply(split(valid_readings$pm25, valid_readings$site),
                    function(x) unlist(exposure_summary(x))))
round(by_site, 2)
```

```{r function-tests}
exposure_summary(c(0, 15, 20))               # 15 is not an exceedance
exposure_summary(c(0, 15, 20), limit = 20)
exposure_summary(c("a", "b"))                # text
exposure_summary(numeric(0))                 # empty vector
exposure_summary(c(5, -2, 8))                # negative value
exposure_summary(c(5, NA, 8))                # missing value
exposure_summary(c(5, 8), limit = c(10, 20)) # limit of length 2
exposure_summary(c(5, 8), limit = -1)        # negative limit
```

The percentage uses `length(x)` as the denominator, that is, the number of
**valid readings passed to the function**, not the rows of the original table.
Here `r nrow(valid_readings)` valid readings enter the summaries, compared with
`r nrow(readings)` rows in `readings`. With `c(0, 15, 20)` and a limit of 15
only the 20 exceeds it (1 of 3, 33.3 %).

# Part 3. SQL queries

All queries use `dbGetQuery()` and run on the **original** data, including the
missing and negative readings.

## 3.1 Connection and tables

```{r sql-setup}
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(con, "readings", readings, row.names = FALSE)
dbWriteTable(con, "sites_info", sites_info, row.names = FALSE)

dbListTables(con)
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_readings FROM readings")
```

## 3.2 Exceedances

> List the readings that exceed 15 µg/m³ (`reading_id`, `site`, `pm25`), from the
> highest to the lowest value; ties are ordered by `reading_id`.

```{r sql-exceedances}
exceedances <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT reading_id, site, pm25
  FROM readings
  WHERE pm25 > 15
  ORDER BY pm25 DESC, reading_id ASC")

head(exceedances, 10)
nrow(exceedances)
```

## 3.3 Exceedances per site, with a check

> Count the exceedances per site, ordered by count (descending) and name. Check
> that the counts add up to the rows of 3.2.

```{r sql-by-site}
exceed_by_site <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT site, COUNT(*) AS n_exceedances
  FROM readings
  WHERE pm25 > 15
  GROUP BY site
  ORDER BY n_exceedances DESC, site ASC")
exceed_by_site

sum(exceed_by_site$n_exceedances) == nrow(exceedances)
```

## 3.4 Exceedance rate with `CASE` and `HAVING`

> For each site, compute the number of valid readings, the mean and the
> **percentage of valid readings above the limit**. Keep only the sites whose
> mean is above 12 µg/m³. Valid means non-missing and non-negative.

```{r sql-rate}
site_stats <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT site,
         COUNT(*)                                             AS n_valid,
         ROUND(AVG(pm25), 2)                                  AS mean_pm25,
         ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN pm25 > 15 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
               / COUNT(*), 1)                                 AS pct_exceed
  FROM readings
  WHERE pm25 >= 0
  GROUP BY site
  HAVING AVG(pm25) > 12
  ORDER BY pct_exceed DESC")
site_stats
```

`WHERE` filters **rows** before grouping (here, the invalid readings), while
`HAVING` filters **groups** after the aggregation (here, the sites by their
mean). The `CASE` expression turns each reading into 1 (exceedance) or 0, so its
sum is the number of exceedances.

## 3.5 Joining a second table

> Using `sites_info`, count the exceedances by zone type.

```{r sql-join}
exceed_by_zone <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT s.zone_type, COUNT(*) AS n_exceedances
  FROM readings AS r
  JOIN sites_info AS s ON r.site = s.site
  WHERE r.pm25 > 15
  GROUP BY s.zone_type
  ORDER BY n_exceedances DESC")
exceed_by_zone
```

## 3.6 Visualisation and limitation

```{r sql-plot}
all_sites <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT site,
         COUNT(*) AS n_valid,
         ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN pm25 > 15 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
               / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_exceed
  FROM readings
  WHERE pm25 >= 0
  GROUP BY site
  ORDER BY pct_exceed DESC")

ggplot(all_sites, aes(x = reorder(site, -pct_exceed), y = pct_exceed)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Share of valid readings above the WHO 24-h guideline",
       x = "Monitoring site",
       y = "Readings above 15 ug/m3 (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r sql-values, include=FALSE}
top    <- all_sites[1, ]
bottom <- all_sites[nrow(all_sites), ]
```

**Interpretation.** **`r top$site`** has the highest share of exceedances
(`r top$pct_exceed` % of its `r top$n_valid` valid readings) and
**`r bottom$site`** the lowest (`r bottom$pct_exceed` %). The ranking
follows the typical level assigned to each site when the synthetic data were
generated, so with real data the same query would be used to identify the
sites that need attention first.

**Limitation.** The percentages are computed on **valid readings only**, and
each site loses a different number of readings to missing values and sensor
errors. A site can look cleaner simply because its worst days were not recorded,
especially if sensors tend to fail during pollution episodes (data that are
*not* missing at random). The number of valid readings (`n_valid`) should always
be reported next to the percentage.

```{r sql-close}
dbDisconnect(con)
```

# Part 4. Probability and simulation

## 4.1 Binomial model: exceedance days in a month

> At one site, each day exceeds the guideline with probability 0.12,
> independently of the other days. Over a 30-day month, compute the probability
> of exactly 5 exceedance days and of 8 or more.

**Model.** Let *X* be the number of exceedance days in 30 days. Then
*X* ~ B(30, 0.12), assuming a fixed number of days, two outcomes per day
(exceedance or not), independent days and a constant daily probability. (In
practice consecutive days are correlated, so this is a simplification.)

```{r binom}
n_days <- 30
p_day  <- 0.12

p_exact5   <- dbinom(5, n_days, p_day)
p_atleast8 <- pbinom(7, n_days, p_day, lower.tail = FALSE)  # P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)

c(exactly_5 = p_exact5, at_least_8 = p_atleast8)
```

## 4.2 Poisson model: smoke episodes

> Wildfire-smoke episodes affect the area at a constant average rate of 0.8 per
> month. Compute the probability of no episode in 3 months and of at least 4
> episodes in 6 months. Justify the parameter of each interval.

**Model.** Let *N* be the number of episodes in an interval. For a homogeneous
Poisson process, *N* ~ Poisson(λ) with λ = rate × duration, assuming a constant
rate, independent counts in separate intervals and events occurring one at a
time.

- 3 months: λ = 0.8 × 3 = 2.4
- 6 months: λ = 0.8 × 6 = 4.8

```{r pois}
lambda_3m <- 0.8 * 3
lambda_6m <- 0.8 * 6

p_none_3m    <- dpois(0, lambda_3m)
p_atleast4_6 <- ppois(3, lambda_6m, lower.tail = FALSE)     # P(N >= 4) = 1 - P(N <= 3)

c(none_in_3_months = p_none_3m, at_least_4_in_6_months = p_atleast4_6)
```

## 4.3 Normal model: a station's daily mean

> The daily mean PM2.5 at a station is modelled as N(12, 4²) µg/m³ (mean 12,
> standard deviation 4). Compute the probability of exceeding 15 µg/m³ and the
> value exceeded only 5 % of the days.

```{r normal}
p_exceed_normal <- pnorm(15, mean = 12, sd = 4, lower.tail = FALSE)
q95_normal      <- qnorm(0.95, mean = 12, sd = 4)

c(P_above_15 = p_exceed_normal, percentile_95 = q95_normal)
```

For a continuous variable, `P(X > 15) = P(X >= 15)`, so no adjustment of the
limit is needed (unlike the discrete cases above).

## 4.4 Simulation versus exact values

> Simulate 10,000 repetitions of each model, estimate the five probabilities
> above and compare them with the exact values. Plot the theoretical
> probability functions of the two discrete models.

```{r simulation}
set.seed(11)
n_rep <- 10000

sim_binom <- rbinom(n_rep, n_days, p_day)
sim_pois3 <- rpois(n_rep, lambda_3m)
sim_pois6 <- rpois(n_rep, lambda_6m)
sim_norm  <- rnorm(n_rep, mean = 12, sd = 4)

comparison <- data.frame(
  event     = c("X = 5", "X >= 8", "N(3 months) = 0", "N(6 months) >= 4", "Mean > 15"),
  exact     = c(p_exact5, p_atleast8, p_none_3m, p_atleast4_6, p_exceed_normal),
  estimated = c(mean(sim_binom == 5), mean(sim_binom >= 8),
                mean(sim_pois3 == 0), mean(sim_pois6 >= 4),
                mean(sim_norm > 15))
)
comparison$difference <- comparison$estimated - comparison$exact
comparison[, -1] <- round(comparison[, -1], 4)
comparison
```

Each probability is estimated as the **proportion of repetitions** in which the
event occurs. The largest absolute difference is
`r max(abs(comparison$difference))`. The estimates are close to the exact values
but not identical because they are random; they change with the seed and
converge to the exact values as the number of repetitions grows (law of large
numbers).

```{r pmf-plot}
x <- 0:20
pmf <- rbind(
  data.frame(model = "Exceedance days in 30 days (Binomial)",
             count = x, probability = dbinom(x, n_days, p_day),
             in_event = x >= 8),
  data.frame(model = "Smoke episodes in 6 months (Poisson)",
             count = x, probability = dpois(x, lambda_6m),
             in_event = x >= 4)
)

ggplot(pmf, aes(x = count, y = probability, fill = in_event)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "steelblue", `TRUE` = "firebrick"),
                    labels = c("Outside the event", "Inside the event")) +
  labs(x = "Count", y = "Probability", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The red bars are the values that make up each event (8 or more exceedance days;
at least 4 episodes in six months); the sum of their heights is the probability
computed in 4.1 and 4.2.

## 4.5 Sampling without replacement: filter cartridges

> A batch holds 50 filter cartridges, 6 of them defective. An inspector draws 8
> cartridges at random. Estimate by simulation the probability of finding at
> least 2 defective ones, drawing **without** and **with** replacement, and
> compare with the exact values. Explain why the binomial model is not exact
> without replacement.

```{r hypergeom}
batch <- c(rep(1, 6), rep(0, 44))   # 1 = defective, 0 = good

set.seed(5)
sim_without <- replicate(10000, sum(sample(batch, 8, replace = FALSE)))
sim_with    <- replicate(10000, sum(sample(batch, 8, replace = TRUE)))

exact_binom <- pbinom(1, 8, 6 / 50, lower.tail = FALSE)      # with replacement
exact_hyper <- phyper(1, 6, 44, 8, lower.tail = FALSE)       # without replacement

data.frame(
  case = c("Without replacement (simulation)", "With replacement (simulation)",
           "Hypergeometric (exact)", "Binomial (exact)"),
  probability = round(c(mean(sim_without >= 2), mean(sim_with >= 2),
                        exact_hyper, exact_binom), 4)
)
```

Without replacement, every cartridge drawn leaves the batch, so the composition
of what remains changes at each draw: after a defective cartridge is removed,
the probability that the next one is defective drops from 6/50 to 5/49. The
draws are therefore **not independent** and the probability is **not constant**,
which violates both binomial assumptions. The exact model is the
**hypergeometric** distribution (`r round(exact_hyper, 4)`), slightly different
from the binomial value (`r round(exact_binom, 4)`). The binomial becomes a good
approximation when the batch is much larger than the sample drawn.
